topic: Binary Counting and the Towers of Hanoi: The Mathematical Secret

outline.topic: Binary Counting and the Towers of Hanoi: The Mathematical Secret

sections.title: The Binary Language (Prerequisite)
sections.content: Introduce binary (base-2) as a system using only 0 and 1. Explain that each digit position represents a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8...). Visualize this using 'Light Switches': ON=1, OFF=0.
sections.example: A 3-bit system: 001 (1), 010 (2), 011 (3), 100 (4). Animation: 3 switches toggling like a dance.

sections.title: The Towers of Hanoi Puzzle
sections.content: Define the goal: Move a stack of N disks from Peg A to Peg C, moving only one at a time and never placing a larger disk on a smaller one.
sections.example: A monkey trying to move a 3-disk 'banana pyramid' from one tree to another following the strict rules.

sections.title: Mapping Moves to Binary
sections.content: Explain the surprising link: The sequence of disk moves corresponds exactly to the binary counting sequence. The number of moves required for N disks is 2^N - 1.
sections.example: For 3 disks: 2^3 - 1 = 7 moves. Animation showing the move number (1-7) appearing as binary numbers (001 to 111) alongside the disk movement.

sections.title: The Algorithmic Logic
sections.content: Explain that the n-th disk moves exactly once, at step 2^(n-1). This explains why the rhythm of the puzzle is patterned—the smallest disk moves every other turn.
sections.example: A visual 'Clock' where the small hand (disk 1) moves every tick, the middle hand (disk 2) every 2 ticks, and the large hand (disk 3) every 4 ticks.

sections.title: Summary and Real-world Application
sections.content: Conclude by connecting the puzzle to computer science algorithms (recursion) and data storage. Remind students that binary isn't just counting—it's the 'DNA' of logical movement.
sections.example: Showing a computer chip or a server rack processing data packets as if they were disks in a Hanoi tower.

storyboard.title: The Binary Language (Prerequisite)
lecture_lines: Binary uses only zero and one digits.
Each position represents a power of two.
Light switches visualize binary states perfectly.
animations: Create a sequence of zeros and ones on screen.
Highlight a single bit, color it #FFD700 (Gold).
Flash the bit to signify its importance.

storyboard.title: The Towers of Hanoi Puzzle
lecture_lines: Move disks from start to end peg.
Never place larger disks on smaller ones.
Move one disk at a time only.
animations: Display three pegs with a stack of disks.
Highlight the smallest disk, color it #FF4500 (OrangeRed).
Animate the disk moving from peg A to C.

storyboard.title: Mapping Moves to Binary
lecture_lines: Hanoi moves match the binary sequence.
Three disks require seven total moves.
Binary count zero-zero-one is move one.
Binary count one-one-one is move seven.
The sequence maps binary to disk movement.
animations: Show a disk moving and a binary digit changing.
Synchronize the disk shift with the digit flip.

storyboard.title: The Algorithmic Logic
lecture_lines: Small disks move every other turn.
Middle disks move every four turns.
Large disks move every eight turns.
Smallest disk moves at every odd step.
Movement follows a perfect recursive pattern.
animations: Animate the recursive calls branching out like trees.

storyboard.title: Summary and Real-world Application
lecture_lines: Recursion is the engine of movement.
Binary is the DNA of logic.
Computer chips process data like Hanoi.
animations: Display a computer chip image as.
Superimpose the disk tower logic onto the chip.
